model.title: GridStory control plane and delivery threat model
model.methodology: OWASP four-question threat modeling with STRIDE categorization
scope: workers, outbox, durable jobs, search, cache, and webhook adapters
published REST delivery and application-owned React rendering
signed plugin manifests, tenant grants, lifecycle state, external runtime protocol, and scoped marketplace publisher/release evidence
data governance, legal holds, rights requests, guarded erasure, encrypted exports, customer-managed key references, and placement attestations
read-only CMS source adapters, private migration recipes, dry-run plans, checkpoints, links, receipts, and cutover evidence
consent-aware targeting attributes, audiences, draft/published configuration, hypothetical preview, edge decisions, and cache guidance
governed experiment designs, lifecycle, stateless weighted allocation, aggregate evidence, guardrails, and targeting-draft promotion
bounded published content/component analytics events, normalized lifecycle evidence, release annotations, aggregate metrics, and injected adapter delivery
governed AI policy, immutable prompt versions, scoped allowlisted retrieval, provider-neutral text generation, redaction, budgets, usage receipts, and kill switches
outOfScope: security of application-owned React components after validated data leaves GridStory
cloud, CDN, database, object-store, and network controls not configured by GridStory
package binary hosting/download, scanner-engine internals, publisher business-legitimacy verification, and operating-system/container isolation supplied outside GridStory

customer profile storage, consent collection or legal interpretation, raw analytics warehousing/export, attribution/funnels/cohorts, provider credentials or provider-specific SDKs in core, statistical-significance engines, automatic experiment winner selection or publication, autonomous agents, tools, content mutation, semantic search, provider fallback, or raw AI invocation history

riskModel.scale: likelihood and impact are integers from 1 (low) to 5 (critical)

assumptions: Production deployments terminate TLS and protect databases, queues, object stores, logs, and secret stores with least privilege.
Development identity headers and default secrets are never exposed on a production listener.
Applications validate and safely render application-owned components; GridStory never executes editor-authored JavaScript.
External adapters implement the documented timeouts, redirect, egress, credential, and tenant-scope contracts.

The M5-002 application isolation review verifies canonical scope keys and fail-closed boundaries across persistence, cache, search, assets, jobs, events, audit, and telemetry; production infrastructure policies remain deployment evidence.

Production plugin runtimes are separately operated processes or containers with least-privilege OS, filesystem, network, CPU, and memory policies; the GridStory adapter protocol does not itself provide OS isolation.

Marketplace artifact inspectors are separately authenticated and operated trusted adapters whose policy, evidence storage, availability, and scanner-engine correctness require deployment conformance; a passing result or verified provenance is not a safety guarantee.
CMS migration credentials are read-only, least privilege, and injected by the trusted server runtime; the source stays authoritative and recoverable until an externally operated cutover is accepted.

Applications create and, when permitted, retain an unpredictable token separately for each experiment after consent; external experiment analytics still owns attribution, statistical validity, and retained evidence integrity.

Applications send only anonymous allowlisted analytics events after a valid configured-purpose decision; deployments own public rate controls and provider adapter credentials, retention, deletion, egress, and independently protected diagnostics.

AI provider adapters are composed only in the trusted server runtime, preserve structured instruction/data separation and output limits, honor abort signals where supported, and keep credentials, provider diagnostics, retention, regional processing, and egress policy outside browser, schema, core, persistence, and logs.

threats.title: Cross-tenant object access or mutation
threats.scenario: An attacker supplies another tenant's object ID or scope headers and reaches content, assets, jobs, search results, audit history, or configuration.
mitigations: Require complete scope in request, storage, cache, event, job, audit, and adapter contracts.
Deny by default and authorize the resource action before access.
Run cross-scope conformance tests continuously; production deployments separately verify database and object-store policies.

threats.title: Development identity headers accepted in production
threats.scenario: A public deployment trusts caller-controlled actor, role, or tenant headers and grants administrative access.
mitigations: Keep development header identity explicit and reject actor, role, and principal-type headers in production mode.
Verify backend-held opaque sessions or tenant-bound directory credentials before protected production requests.
Use maintained OIDC/SAML/WebAuthn adapters with one-time durable protocol state; retain trusted-proxy and TLS conformance as deployment evidence.

threats.title: Preview token disclosure or replay
threats.scenario: A leaked preview grant is replayed from another origin or used after revocation to read draft content.
mitigations: Use short-lived HMAC grants bound to audience, full scope, origin, route, mode, and optional entry.
Check origin/source, expiry, revocation, monotonically increasing sequence, and nonce uniqueness.
Never place grants in published URLs or caches.

threats.title: Draft content enters a public cache
threats.scenario: A mixed perspective response or incomplete cache key exposes draft content to anonymous delivery consumers.
mitigations: Force published perspective on public delivery.
Use private, no-store for management, GraphQL, preview, assets, and operations.
Include full scope and exact revision in public cache tags and vary policy.

threats.title: Webhook SSRF or DNS rebinding
threats.scenario: A privileged user supplies a destination that reaches localhost, private infrastructure, metadata services, or redirects to them.
mitigations: Require HTTPS public hosts and reject credentials, localhost, local/reserved literals, and redirects.
Configure a production host allow-list and network egress/DNS controls.
Revalidate the destination at execution time.

threats.title: Forged or replayed outbound event
threats.scenario: A receiver accepts a forged webhook or processes a legitimate durable delivery repeatedly.
mitigations: Sign timestamp and exact raw body with HMAC-SHA256.
Expose immutable delivery and event IDs.
Require receiver freshness checks and delivery-ID deduplication.

threats.title: Malicious or mislabeled asset upload
threats.scenario: A polyglot, active SVG, malware, oversized payload, pixel bomb, or false MIME type reaches storage or a browser.
mitigations: Match server-recorded multipart descriptors and inspect exact bytes.
Verify signatures/type, sanitize SVG, inject malware scanning, and fail closed into immutable quarantine.
Enforce repository byte/declared-dimension limits plus deployment-specific decoded-pixel, decompression, processing, concurrency, and quota limits.

threats.title: Private asset grant leakage or substitution
threats.scenario: A signed asset URL is leaked, altered to another object, cached publicly, or reused beyond its intended lifetime.
mitigations: Bind HMAC grant to complete scope and exact asset/revision with 30-900 second expiry.
Recheck verified state and scope-safe object key at read time.
Return private, no-store with nosniff and SVG sandbox CSP.

threats.title: Archive tampering or cross-scope import
threats.scenario: A crafted logical archive changes history, injects another scope, exceeds capacity, or partially imports before failure.
mitigations: Verify canonical per-entry and aggregate checksums, format/schema versions, and exact target scope.
Offer dry-run/conflict reporting and atomic rollback.
Enforce import bytes, archive entries, per-entry revisions/audit events, and deployment execution limits.

threats.title: GraphQL or query complexity exhaustion
threats.scenario: Nested, broad, aliased, batched, or expensive filters consume excessive CPU, memory, or database work.
mitigations: Limit GraphQL depth to 12; disable batching and subscriptions.
Bound page, filter, sort, and projection inputs.
Bound aliases, field selections, body size, and application-pipeline budgets; require deployment concurrency/rate and introspection policy before GA.

threats.title: Cursor tampering or query-context substitution
threats.scenario: An attacker edits a continuation cursor or reuses it for another scope, perspective, filter, sort, or projection.
mitigations: Sign cursors and bind them to complete scope and canonical query shape.
Use constant-time signature comparison and stable validation errors.
Rotate the cursor secret deliberately.

threats.title: Search perspective or tenant bleed
threats.scenario: An adapter returns another tenant's records, exposes draft data to published search, or serves stale results after publication.
mitigations: Make full scope and perspective mandatory adapter keys.
Put identifiers, not content, in incremental jobs and reload under scope.
Expose scoped rebuild/status and reject mismatched adapter scope, perspective, totals, facets, and repository records.

threats.title: Durable job scope confusion or duplicate effect
threats.scenario: A job payload carries the wrong tenant or stale draft content, a lease is stolen, or retry/replay duplicates an external side effect.
mitigations: Persist full scope separately from bounded payloads and use identifier-only payloads where possible.
Use expiring owner-checked leases and full-scope idempotency keys.
Preserve immutable completion/dead-letter history and create a new identity for replay.

threats.title: Workflow approval or release-policy bypass
threats.scenario: A user self-approves despite separation-of-duties rules, executes an unvalidated/stale release, or overwrites concurrent intent.
mitigations: Authorize distinct transition, approval, schedule, execute, and rollback actions.
Enforce separation of duties and exact expected revisions.
Publish releases atomically after future-state validation and audit every action.

threats.title: Audit tampering, truncation, or log injection
threats.scenario: An attacker alters or removes audit events, injects misleading text, or causes secrets/content to enter operational logs.
mitigations: Hash-chain events within exact scope and checksum exports.
Restrict audit read/export to administrators.
Export bounded structured logs/traces/metrics through an allow-listed Collector pipeline with explicit access, retention, alerting, and incident response; retain audit separately.

threats.title: Signing secret or service credential compromise
threats.scenario: A weak, shared, logged, or unrotated secret permits forged preview, cursor, webhook, asset, or service-account credentials.
mitigations: Use independent high-entropy secrets and constant-time comparisons.
Store service secrets as hashes and support expiry/revocation.
Use a production secret manager, rotation schedule, credential inventory, and emergency revocation runbook.

threats.title: Stored content causes script or markup execution
threats.scenario: Untrusted content, rich text, SVG, component props, or URLs execute in Studio, preview, or the consuming application.
mitigations: Store validated structured data and code-owned component IDs; never execute editor-authored JavaScript.
Validate URL and rich-text contracts and sanitize SVG.
Require context-appropriate output encoding and safe rendering in each consuming application.

threats.title: External adapter failure or compromise
threats.scenario: A cache, search, storage, scanner, identity, or notification adapter leaks scoped data, hangs, returns hostile data, or corrupts state.
mitigations: Keep explicit framework-neutral interfaces and pass complete scope.
Validate adapter outputs and fail closed for security-critical scanning/identity.
Set bounded timeouts, retries, circuit breaking, least-privilege credentials, and health telemetry.

threats.title: Resource exhaustion and unbounded retention
threats.scenario: Large bodies, archives, uploads, queries, revisions, jobs, retries, or audit history exhaust memory, disk, database, or worker capacity.
mitigations: Retain existing bounded query, action, retry, and worker-batch limits.
Enforce and benchmark repository body/upload/archive/query/job/plugin limits.
Require deployment concurrency/rate/quota/saturation evidence and product retention policy before GA.
Monitor saturation and fail predictably.

threats.title: Dependency or build artifact compromise
threats.scenario: A malicious dependency, install script, registry response, CI token, or unsigned release modifies shipped packages.
mitigations: Keep lockfile-pinned dependencies and protected CI credentials.
Run OSV/Dependabot review and create reviewed package inventories, checksums, SPDX SBOMs, and GitHub/Sigstore provenance/SBOM attestations.
Document remediation service levels.

threats.title: Transport or proxy misconfiguration
threats.scenario: Missing TLS, unsafe forwarded-header trust, broad CORS, or incorrect origin configuration leaks credentials or changes the perceived caller/origin.
mitigations: Use explicit CORS and preview-origin allow-lists.
Terminate modern TLS and configure trusted proxies explicitly.
Add production configuration validation and deployment conformance checks.

threats.title: Sensitive error or debug disclosure
threats.scenario: Stack traces, internal exceptions, secrets, tokens, content, or database detail are returned to an untrusted caller or logged without redaction.
mitigations: Return stable generic envelopes for unexpected server errors.
Treat known validation errors as bounded client errors.
Export only bounded route/error attributes, omit raw requests and exception detail, and apply a fail-closed Collector allow-list.

threats.title: Malicious, forged, over-granted, or escaped plugin
threats.scenario: An attacker installs a forged or incompatible package, expands a tenant grant, invokes a revoked plugin, crosses tenant scope, or uses plugin code to reach ambient control-plane authority or exhaust the host.
mitigations: Verify canonical Ed25519 manifests, exact SHA-256 artifact digests, publisher trust, and SDK/protocol compatibility before installation.

For marketplace installs, require current publisher trust, immutable approved release state, and a current exact-artifact passing review before handing off to disabled installation with no automatic grants.
Authorize tenant-scoped lifecycle actions and require granted constrained capabilities to be a subset of the signed request.
Never import plugin modules; use an injected external runtime with bounded health/invocation messages, rate, time, input, and output limits, and fail closed when no runtime is configured.
Retain immutable lifecycle evidence and support immediate tenant disablement and revocation; separately harden the operating-system/container boundary.

threats.title: Database backup disclosure, tampering, or unsafe restore
threats.scenario: A whole-database artifact is exposed, corrupted, replaced, restored over a live target, or accepted without proving that the recovered database is complete and compatible.
mitigations: Use database-native consistent snapshots/dumps and verify archive format, byte length, SHA-256, database integrity, and required GridStory tables before restore.
Keep database URLs and passwords out of process arguments and manifests; encrypt artifacts off-host with least-privilege access, retention, and access logging.

Refuse an existing SQLite or non-empty PostgreSQL GridStory target and require exact target-database confirmation; perform production recovery through reviewed isolated restore, verification, and cutover.
Exercise logical restore regularly and provider-managed base-backup plus continuous-WAL PITR against stated RPO/RTO before production acceptance.

threats.title: Governance bypass, overbroad export, or irreversible deletion
threats.scenario: An attacker or mistaken operator crosses scope, exports unlinked personal data, bypasses a hold/restriction, approves their own stale plan, uses an unavailable/wrong-region key, or deletes changed/external resources without recoverable evidence.
mitigations: Authorize read/manage/execute separately against complete scope and inventory only explicit subject/resource links.
Make active holds/restrictions dominate deletion and require a new dry-run after any governance change.
Require another administrator, fresh server-validated reauthentication, exact digest, recent verified backup evidence, and worker-time plan/resource/policy revalidation.
Use narrow processor/KMS/placement adapters, envelope encryption, no plaintext key persistence, fail-closed unsupported resources, and ordered hash-chained receipts/events.

threats.title: CMS source credential disclosure, SSRF, hostile continuation, or source exhaustion
threats.scenario: A malicious configuration or compromised CMS response exposes credentials, redirects or continues to an attacker origin, returns malformed or oversized data, or causes unbounded source reads and persistent private-data leakage.
mitigations: Compose credentials only in the trusted server, require credential-free configured HTTPS base origins, disable redirects, and reject every cross-origin continuation or response URL.
Use provider read-only credentials, bounded response bytes and record counts, strict normalized schemas, redacted stable errors, and no source write methods.
Keep source snapshots, plans, checkpoints, and links in private complete-scope repositories and never expose credentials or mapped private data in plan summaries or telemetry.
Require production egress policy, secret-manager lifecycle, provider audit logs, revocation, and rate/timeout controls as deployment evidence.

threats.title: Migration drift, retry duplication, destructive reconciliation, or false cutover readiness
threats.scenario: A stale or changed plan overwrites manual target work, a crash duplicates an import or advances a checkpoint early, a missing/deleted source record destroys target data, or an incomplete report is represented as traffic-cutover readiness.
mitigations: Require a bounded immutable dry-run with exact effects, blockers, expiry, deterministic digest, project and recipe versions, source checksum, expected target revision, and operator digest confirmation.

Persist a pending deterministic source-to-target link before each write, recover checksum-identical partial writes, finalize receipts before advancing checkpoints, and return the same successful receipt on retry.
Run all target writes through normal schema, reference, workflow, quality, governance, revision, route, and publish gates; fail closed on target/source/recipe/project drift.
Report source deletions, missing mappings, unsupported media, incomplete snapshots, missing targets, and unpublished targets as blockers without automatic deletion or unpublish propagation.

Require a backed-up shadow environment, full reconciliation, retained source traffic authority, and an external application/SEO/analytics/infrastructure cutover checklist; a content report never changes traffic.

threats.title: Forged, stale, or overclaimed marketplace publisher identity
threats.scenario: An attacker registers a deceptive identity, replays or guesses a DNS challenge, approves their own publisher, substitutes a key, or continues installing releases after publisher trust is suspended.
mitigations: Validate stable identities, registrable domains, same-domain HTTPS ownership links, and Ed25519 public keys before persistence.
Use unpredictable bounded exact-name DNS TXT challenges that expire and record only an observed possession signal.
Require a different authenticated operator to approve evidence with a reason/reference and allow immediate publisher suspension.
Revalidate current publisher state, exact key ID, signature, release review, and immutable digest before every marketplace installation; omit challenges and key bodies from catalog summaries.

threats.title: Forged, stale, incomplete, or overtrusted marketplace release review
threats.scenario: A compromised or unavailable inspector returns evidence for different bytes, hides unsafe inventory or vulnerabilities, supplies stale provenance, or causes a human to treat a badge or scan as proof of safety and approve or install a risky release.
mitigations: Never execute or import package code in the control plane; use only a configured trusted inspector and fail closed on absence or error.

Bind review to the exact signed manifest, digest, size, publisher/key, inspector identity/version, evidence reference, completion time, SPDX inventory, provenance subject, malware, vulnerability, license, and archive-inventory results.
Block stale, mismatched, missing, unknown, detected, denied, high/critical, traversal, install-script, or native-binary evidence and expose capability requests as human-review warnings.

Require a distinct release approver, retain rejected/yanked history, install disabled with no automatic grants, and state that identity, provenance, scanning, support, installation, and runtime safety are separate signals.

threats.title: Personal-data overcollection, consent bypass, draft leakage, or targeting cache confusion
threats.scenario: An attacker or misconfigured application submits identifying or unbounded traits, claims consent that is absent or denied, bypasses a GPC-sensitive purpose, evaluates draft policy publicly, crosses tenant scope, or omits a varying input/revision from a shared cache key so one visitor or tenant receives another decision.
mitigations: Accept only declared boolean or finite-enum attributes, reject unknown keys, types, values, purposes, duplicate priorities, and dangling rule or variant references, and never persist decision inputs or profiles.

Require purposes on every personal attribute, make personal and authentication inputs private-cache only, honor explicit denied consent, and suppress only purposes configured to honor a received GPC signal.

Authorize management and hypothetical preview separately, keep them private and no-store, publish only the exact optimistic draft revision, and expose anonymous evaluation only from the published snapshot.

Evaluate deterministic first-match rules with a required fallback and emit shared guidance only when every possible input is bounded public and consent-independent; bind the key to complete scope, locale, published revision, resource, and every decision input.

Keep the HTTP decision response private/no-store, omit raw values from explanations, bound configuration/context sizes, and document customer responsibility for consent collection, legal interpretation, source normalization, CDN configuration, and purge operations.

threats.title: Experiment assignment, evidence, guardrail, or promotion abuse
threats.scenario: An attacker or misconfigured application reuses an identifying token, allocates without consent, changes a running design or targeting baseline, overlaps experiments, submits incomplete or forged aggregates, bypasses sample/allocation/metric guardrails, leaks assignments through caches, or promotes/publishes an unsupported treatment.
threats.owner: Experimentation, privacy, analytics, and delivery owner
mitigations: Authorize experiment read, manage, metric, and promotion operations separately against complete scope; keep management private/no-store and retain optimistic actor/reason/time evidence.

Validate exact 10,000-basis-point designs, one primary metric, declared purpose and targeting references; make started designs immutable, pin the published targeting revision, and reject active placement overlap or drift.

Require application-generated random per-experiment UUIDs after consent, hash them only with complete scope/experiment/revision, never persist or echo tokens/buckets/raw context, set no cookie, and make allocation responses no-store with an ordinary targeting fallback.

Accept only complete bounded aggregate snapshots with immutable identity and external SHA-256 evidence digest; enforce allocation deviation, every per-variant sample minimum, and absolute guardrails, automatically pausing a running failure.

Require completed state, elapsed duration, a retained passing snapshot, unchanged control targeting, explicit non-control choice, and primary-direction improvement; atomically update only the targeting draft and make no statistical-significance, automatic-winner, or publication claim.

Require external evidence-store integrity, metric/attribution/statistics review, token-retention policy, rate controls, consent/legal review, and application cache/render isolation as deployment evidence.

threats.title: Fabricated, identifying, replayed, or unavailable content analytics
threats.scenario: An attacker or misconfigured application sends identifying/free-form, draft, stale, cross-scope, duplicated, old/future, or consent-disallowed analytics evidence; exhausts aggregate/job cardinality; forges lifecycle/release correlation; or uses a slow, removed, unavailable, or hostile provider adapter to leak secrets, block publication, lose retry evidence, or corrupt operational metrics.
threats.owner: Analytics, privacy, operations, and delivery owner
mitigations: Accept only a strict closed content-view/component-view/component-interaction union with bounded UUID/time/token fields; reject arbitrary properties and all visitor, account, session, assignment, URL, referrer, IP, user-agent, device, draft, and preview values.

Derive complete scope only from validated delivery context, require the configured purpose grant, honor received GPC, bound age/future skew, and prove the exact content ID/type/revision is the current published pointer before durable acceptance.

Normalize server lifecycle only from the complete-scope transactional outbox, enqueue release annotations only after authoritative persisted publication/rollback, and never reverse content or release truth when analytics enqueue/delivery fails.

Use idempotent process receipts, optimistic complete-scope memory/SQLite/PostgreSQL aggregates, explicit cardinality/truncation limits, independent leased delivery jobs, retries/dead letters/replay, and a private operations-authorized report that omits receipt IDs and raw evidence.

Inject adapters only at trusted server composition, keep credentials/providers out of schema/core, validate adapter IDs, replace thrown diagnostics with a stable generic retained error, and require deployment TLS/egress/timeout/rate/retention/deletion/access/alert controls.

Treat bounded counters and release annotations as operational correlation only; require separately governed attribution, bot/late-event policy, statistical methodology, evidence authenticity, retention, and causality review before higher-stakes use.

threats.title: Prompt injection, scoped-source disclosure, unbounded spend, or stale AI disablement
threats.scenario: An editor, hostile content source, tenant, or external model provider injects instructions or sensitive values; requests another scope, draft, type, or field; replays request IDs; selects an unapproved model; under-reports metering; exhausts cost/token/request limits; leaks provider diagnostics; returns malformed or oversized output; or races a kill switch so stale output is released or treated as authoritative content.
threats.owner: AI governance, security, platform, and editorial owner
mitigations: Authorize private AI read, manage, and execute operations separately; derive complete scope from trusted context, reauthorize every source as content.read, and reject missing, cross-scope, disallowed-type, disallowed-field, draft/published-perspective, model, or active-prompt mismatches.

Persist one bounded complete-scope optimistic document; keep prompt versions immutable, active pointers explicit, state changes accountable, request UUIDs one-use, daily usage bounded, and invocation receipts metadata-only with no user input, source text, provider output, or thrown diagnostics.

Send only structured text requests with fixed prompt instructions separated from untrusted user/source data; allow explicit source IDs and positive field paths only, redact credentials/email/phone/IP before egress and after response, validate all estimates/results, label output untrusted, and expose no tools or content mutation path.

Reserve requests, estimated input, maximum output, and conservative cost atomically before provider execution; never refund failures or over-reservation violations, reconcile successful usage downward only, reject duplicates and exhausted budgets, and require separately validated provider billing reconciliation.

Inject provider adapters only at trusted server composition; omit tenant routing and credentials from the provider request, bound time/input/output/source/model values, abort on timeout, replace provider failures with generic errors, and require deployment TLS, egress, secrets, retention, regional, rate, billing, and incident controls.

Check enabled state and exact active prompt/model before retrieval, during reservation immediately before the provider, and during optimistic success settlement; discard and mark failed any response whose gateway, prompt, or model changed, so an in-flight kill switch prevents output release.

threats.title: AI proposal poisoning, non-human approval, stale handoff, or semantic index scope bleed
threats.scenario: A provider returns malformed, incomplete, duplicate, oversized, disallowed-field, or schema-invalid suggestion data; an actor fabricates evaluation/provenance, approves through a service account, reviews twice, applies against a changed draft, or treats approval as publication; or a semantic adapter indexes non-allowlisted sensitive fields, accepts a poisoned job/query, returns a cross-scope, wrong-perspective/model/field, duplicate, non-finite, unauthorized, or stale revision hit, leaks diagnostics, or makes derived vectors authoritative backup data.
threats.owner: AI governance, security, platform, search, and editorial owner
mitigations: Require ai.execute plus ordinary target/source reads for generation, ai.review only for publisher/admin user principals, and content.read again for review and every semantic result; reject service-account/anonymous review and allow only one pending-review transition.

Bind each enabled action to one known prompt/content type and unique top-level text/slug targets; require the fixed gridstory.authoring-suggestions.v1 contract, complete stop result, bounded unique declared changes, exact current target revision, ordinary complete candidate validation, and every deterministic rule before a proposal can be reviewed.

Persist bounded redacted suggested values plus exact action/request/prompt/model/target/source revision, usage/redaction, actor/time, evaluation, and one review record; retain no raw provider JSON, rendered prompt, source values, semantic query, embedding/vector, or adapter diagnostics.

Treat approval as review evidence only; recheck the exact target revision, mark stale rather than approve on drift, expose approved values in Studio only as visible dirty local edits, and require the normal content save, workflow, quality, and publication path afterward.

Index only positively configured top-level text/slug fields at configured perspectives, redact before the injected tenant-aware adapter, keep durable job payloads identifier-only, and treat adapter vectors/indexes as disposable derived state rebuilt from authoritative content.

Redact and bound private semantic queries, validate adapter identity/model/index metadata and every hit's complete scope, perspective, unique ID, finite score, content type, positive field provenance, current revision, and content authorization; fail the whole request closed on hostile or stale evidence and replace thrown adapter diagnostics with generic errors.

Keep authoring and semantic policy complete-scope, optimistic, bounded, private/no-store, and disabled by default; ship no provider/vector SDK or credentials, and require deployment TLS, egress, secrets, retention, deletion, model/index quality, availability, rate, and incident evidence.
